changes._why: LENGTH counts bytes; the request counts characters (CHAR_LENGTH); the columns the request names
changes.sql:
SELECT film_id, title, CHAR_LENGTH(description) AS characters
FROM film_text
ORDER BY characters DESC, film_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: sorted by the rounded average, so close averages tied and the wrong actor could rank higher
request: For each actor, take the average `length` of the films they appear in, through `film_actor`.
Show the five actors with the largest average: their `actor_id`, `first_name`, `last_name` and the average rounded to two decimal places, the largest first.
The order uses the average itself, not the rounded one; break ties by `actor_id`.
changes.sql:
SELECT a.*, ROUND(AVG(f.length), 2) AS average_length
FROM actor a
         JOIN film_actor fa ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id
         JOIN film f ON f.film_id = fa.film_id
GROUP BY a.actor_id
ORDER BY AVG(f.length) DESC, a.actor_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: a NULL length fell into ELSE 'long'; Codex's own group for it, over Claude's leaving it out
changes.title: how many films are short, medium, long, or of unknown length
request: Put each film in one of four groups by its `length`: `short` under 60 minutes, `medium` from 60 to 120 minutes, `long` over 120 minutes, and `unknown` where `length` is NULL.
Show each group with its number of films, from the shortest group to the longest, `unknown` last.
A `CASE` expression makes the group, and the query groups by it; a NULL length passes no comparison, so it needs a test of its own.
changes.sql:
SELECT CASE
           WHEN length IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
           WHEN length < 60 THEN 'short'
           WHEN length <= 120 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'long'
           END  AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS films
FROM film
GROUP BY size
ORDER BY CASE size WHEN 'short' THEN 1 WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 WHEN 'long' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END

changes._why: equal counts do not show the same films; film_text has no foreign key to film
request: `film_text` keeps a copy of each film's title and description, for the full-text index; triggers on `film` keep it up to date.
Count the rows of `film_text` and of `film`, the films without a `film_text` row, and the `film_text` rows without a film, in one row.
Equal counts alone would not show that the two hold the same films; `film_text` has no foreign key to `film`.
changes.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM film_text) AS film_text,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM film)      AS film,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM film f
        WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM film_text ft WHERE ft.film_id = f.film_id)) AS without_text,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)
        FROM film_text ft
        WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM film f WHERE f.film_id = ft.film_id)) AS without_film

changes._why: an actor without a film has a NULL film_info, which fell into a NULL group instead of 0
request: Count the categories of each actor's `film_info` as in SAKILA_ACTOR_INFO_I_02, then group the actors by that number.
Show each number of categories with the number of actors, the most categories first.
The groups are formed on a computed value, not on a column; an actor without a film has a NULL `film_info`, counted as 0 categories.
changes.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(CHAR_LENGTH(film_info) - CHAR_LENGTH(REPLACE(film_info, ':', '')), 0) AS categories, COUNT(*) AS actors
FROM actor_info
GROUP BY categories
ORDER BY categories DESC

changes._why: a NULL film_info made the comparison UNKNOWN, so such an actor was never checked
request: Check the view against the tables it is built on.

For each actor, compare the number of categories in `film_info`, counted as in SAKILA_ACTOR_INFO_I_02, with the number of distinct categories of the actor's films, counted from `film_actor` and `film_category` by a correlated subquery; a NULL `film_info` counts as 0, so an actor without a film is checked too.
Show the `actor_id`, the `first_name` and the `last_name` of the actors where the two differ, ordered by `actor_id`.
The installed data has none.
changes.sql:
SELECT ai.*
FROM actor_info ai
WHERE COALESCE(CHAR_LENGTH(ai.film_info) - CHAR_LENGTH(REPLACE(ai.film_info, ':', '')), 0)
          <> (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT fc.category_id)
              FROM film_actor fa
                       JOIN film_category fc ON fc.film_id = fa.film_id
              WHERE fa.actor_id = ai.actor_id)
ORDER BY ai.actor_id

changes._why: SELECT *, LEFT(...) AS film_info gave two film_info columns, the first the whole string
changes.sql:
SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name, LEFT(film_info, 80) AS film_info
FROM actor_info
WHERE actor_id = 1

changes._why: the lowest and highest were hard-coded; title is not unique, so LIMIT 10 needs film_id
request: Find the films whose `rental_rate` is the lowest of all films and whose `replacement_cost` is the highest of all films; in the installed data those are `0.99` and `29.99`.
Show their `film_id`, `title`, `rental_rate` and `replacement_cost`, ordered by title, then by `film_id`, and keep the first ten.
changes.sql:
SELECT *
FROM film
WHERE rental_rate = (SELECT MIN(rental_rate) FROM film)
  AND replacement_cost = (SELECT MAX(replacement_cost) FROM film)
ORDER BY title, film_id
LIMIT 10

changes._why: the default collation ignores case, as does upd_film, so a case-only change was exactly what the check missed
request: Join `film_text` to `film` by the film id, and find the films whose two titles are not exactly the same, letter case included: the `film_id`, the film's `title` and the `film_text` title.
The default collation ignores case, and so does the `upd_film` trigger; `COLLATE utf8mb4_bin` compares the characters as they are.
The triggers keep the titles the same, so the installed data has none.
changes.sql:
SELECT f.*, ft.*
FROM film f
         JOIN film_text ft ON ft.film_id = f.film_id
WHERE ft.title COLLATE utf8mb4_bin <> f.title
ORDER BY f.film_id

changes._why: no Basic exercise shows that COUNT(column) skips NULLs; guards the populated columns other exercises assume
changes.title: how many films lack each optional value
request: `film` has five columns that may be NULL: `description`, `release_year`, `length`, `rating` and `special_features`.
Count, in one row, all the films and, for each of the five, the films where it is NULL.
`COUNT(column)` skips NULLs, so `COUNT(*) - COUNT(column)` is the number of NULLs.
changes.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                           AS films,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(description)      AS no_description,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(release_year)     AS no_release_year,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(length)           AS no_length,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(rating)           AS no_rating,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(special_features) AS no_special_features
FROM film

changes._why: no exercise tells the copies a store owns from the copies it has on the shelf now
changes.title: the copies of a film at each store, and how many are in
request: For the film `1`, show every store with how many copies of the film it owns and how many are in now.
A copy is out while it has a rental whose `return_date` is NULL; a store with no copy shows zeros.
The film goes into the outer join, so every store stays; a `NOT EXISTS` tells a copy that is in.
changes.sql:
SELECT s.store_id,
       COUNT(i.inventory_id) AS copies,
       COUNT(CASE
                 WHEN i.inventory_id IS NOT NULL
                     AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                                     FROM rental r
                                     WHERE r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
                                       AND r.return_date IS NULL) THEN 1
           END)              AS copies_in
FROM store s
         LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.store_id = s.store_id AND i.film_id = 1
GROUP BY s.store_id
ORDER BY s.store_id

changes._why: FILM_B_04 tests one member of the SET column; counting every member means turning the set into rows
changes.title: how many films have each special feature
request: `special_features` is a `SET` of `Trailers`, `Commentaries`, `Deleted Scenes` and `Behind the Scenes`.
For each of the four, count the films whose `special_features` hold it, and show each feature with its count, the most first; ties are ordered by the feature.
A derived table lists the members, and `FIND_IN_SET` joins each to the films that hold it.
changes.sql:
SELECT sf.feature, COUNT(f.film_id) AS films
FROM (SELECT 'Trailers' AS feature
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'Commentaries'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'Deleted Scenes'
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 'Behind the Scenes') sf
         LEFT JOIN film f ON FIND_IN_SET(sf.feature, f.special_features) > 0
GROUP BY sf.feature
ORDER BY films DESC, sf.feature

changes._why: upd_film compares the description with !=, never true against a NULL, so a description set or cleared never reaches film_text
changes.title: the films whose film_text description differs from their description
request: Join `film_text` to `film` by the film id, and find the films whose two descriptions are not exactly the same, a NULL on one side and a value on the other counting as different.
The `upd_film` trigger compares them with `!=`, which is never true when one side is NULL; `<=>` is the comparison that is.
The installed data has none.
changes.sql:
SELECT f.*, ft.*
FROM film f
         JOIN film_text ft ON ft.film_id = f.film_id
WHERE NOT (ft.description COLLATE utf8mb4_bin <=> f.description)
ORDER BY f.film_id

changes._why: SAKILA_FILM_TEXT_A_02 relies on no two titles sharing a first word, which the DDL does not enforce; a check guards it
changes.title: the first words that start more than one title
request: SAKILA_FILM_TEXT_A_02 chains the titles by their words, which works only if no two titles share a first word; nothing in the schema says so.

Group the titles of `film_text` by their first word, and show each first word that starts more than one title, with its number of titles, ordered by the word; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT SUBSTRING_INDEX(title, ' ', 1) AS first_word, COUNT(*) AS titles
FROM film_text
GROUP BY first_word
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY first_word

changes._why: no exercise joins one table twice under two aliases, as the two foreign keys from film to language ask
changes.title: the first five films with the names of their language and original language
request: `film` refers to `language` twice: by `language_id`, and by `original_language_id`, which may be NULL.
Show the first five films by `film_id`, each with the name of its language and the name of its original language, NULL where it has none.
`language` joins twice, under two aliases, the second by an outer join so that no film drops out.
changes.sql:
SELECT f.film_id, f.title, l.name AS language, ol.name AS original_language
FROM film f
         JOIN language l ON l.language_id = f.language_id
         LEFT JOIN language ol ON ol.language_id = f.original_language_id
ORDER BY f.film_id
LIMIT 5

changes._why: LANGUAGE has no Advanced exercise; Claude's (both roles, every language) over Codex's, which ranked by original_language_id, NULL for every film in the data
changes.title: how many films use each language, as language and as original language
changes.file_header: Exercises at the advanced level on language: references turned into rows with UNION ALL, and counted under conditions. Each poses a question, answers it, and shows what the installed data gives back.
request: For every language, even one no film uses, count the films that use it as their `language_id` and the films that use it as their `original_language_id`, both in one row, ordered by `language_id`.
A `UNION ALL` turns the two references into rows, each tagged with its role, and a `COUNT` of a `CASE` counts each role.
changes.sql:
SELECT l.*,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN u.role = 'language' THEN 1 END) AS as_language,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN u.role = 'original' THEN 1 END) AS as_original_language
FROM language l
         LEFT JOIN (SELECT language_id, 'language' AS role
                    FROM film
                    UNION ALL
                    SELECT original_language_id, 'original'
                    FROM film
                    WHERE original_language_id IS NOT NULL) u ON u.language_id = l.language_id
GROUP BY l.language_id
ORDER BY l.language_id

changes._why: film_info is a GROUP_CONCAT, cut at group_concat_max_len; the exercises that count colons in it assume nothing was cut
changes.title: the actors whose film_info may be cut by GROUP_CONCAT
request: `film_info` is built by `GROUP_CONCAT`, which cuts its result at `group_concat_max_len` bytes, 1024 by default, without an error.
Find the actors whose `film_info` is as long as that limit, so that it may have been cut: the `actor_id`, the `first_name`, the `last_name` and the length in bytes, ordered by `actor_id`.
SAKILA_ACTOR_INFO_I_02, I_03 and A_01 count the colons in `film_info`, which is right only if nothing was cut; the check passes when nothing comes back.
changes.sql:
SELECT actor_id, first_name, last_name, LENGTH(film_info) AS film_info_bytes
FROM actor_info
WHERE LENGTH(film_info) >= @@group_concat_max_len
ORDER BY actor_id
